Your company wants to move its coding agents from developer laptops to a shared GKE cluster, for persistence, scale, and governance. Each of those agent sessions stays open all day but works only part of it, and how you run them decides how much of your node bill pays for waiting.
By the end of this article, you will know why an agent session needs a different runtime than a web request, how Agent Substrate and AX run sessions on GKE, and how to identify cost optimization opportunities in your GKE node pools. This article assumes you know Kubernetes Pods and node pools. If not, check out the
GKE overview
.
Agent sessions wait between prompts
A web request lasts milliseconds. The server answers it, keeps nothing, and serves the next one, so Kubernetes scales a web app by its traffic: more requests, more Pods.
An agent session works another way. A coding agent's workspace can stay open for the developer's whole workday: it keeps its memory and its files between prompts, and it works only after a prompt arrives.
Figure 1. A request ends in milliseconds and keeps nothing. An agent session stay

When one Pod per session costs less
Overcommit changes the comparison. If your Pods request less CPU than their limit, Kubernetes places them by their requests. A Pod that requests 0.25 vCPU with a 1 vCPU limit packs 12 to a node (its 1 GiB of memory caps it there), so the same 100 coding agents fit on 9 nodes, fewer than our parked pool. Agent Substrate can overcommit too, through the capacity you declare on the worker pool, and our cost model does not price that case.
Figure 5. The monthly node bill for 100 coding agents by Pod CPU request, from the cost model. Parked sessions keep their full CPU limit in both groups.
Overcommit has the same cost on both sides: agents share CPU and slow down when their neighbors are busy, during builds and tests. Compare like with like before you decide to park: Pods and actors with the same CPU guarantee.
Get started today
Back to the shared cluster. Agents are sessions, not requests: size the warm pool for the sessions that hold a worker, not the sessions that are open.
We would park long lived sessions that wait most of the hour, and keep one Pod per session when developers prompt more than about 4 times an hour. Size the warm pool for working time plus a short idle timeout at your busiest hour, and compare with your current Pods at the same CPU guarantee before you park.

Microbenchmarks are most useful for CPU work that is run many times in your app,
also known as
hot code paths
. Good examples are
RecyclerView
scrolling with
one item shown at a time, data conversions or processing, and other pieces of
code that get used repeatedly.
Other types of code are more difficult to measure with the Microbenchmark
library. Because benchmarks run in a loop, any code that isn't run frequently or
performs differently when called multiple times might not be a good fit for
benchmarking.

benchmark might measure only the performance of the layout cache. To avoid this,

Obtain consistent benchmarks
Clocks on mobile devices dynamically change from high state, for performance, to
low state, to save power or when the device gets hot. These varying clocks can
make your benchmark numbers vary widely, so the library provides ways to deal
with this issue.

We recommend you
profile your code
before writing a benchmark. This helps
you find expensive operations that are worth optimizing. It can also show why
the operations are slow by showing what is happening while they run, such as

calling into an expensive function, like bitmap decoding.
